entries.title: Everyone's adopting AI agents. Almost no one can prove the ROI. Here's why
entries.summary: Amber Roberts, Staff Technical Marketing Manager at Databricks, has spent the last...
entries.content:
Databricks Staff Technical Marketing Manager Amber Roberts on why the old definition of productivity is breaking down, what business context actually buys you, and the mistake most companies make when they try to scale AI agents.

  • Productivity used to mean how much work one person could do alone. In an agentic world, it means how much a person can do with a team of AI assistants working alongside them, without sacrificing quality.
  • The AI "ROI gap" exists because the people buying AI and the people using it are often different, and most organizations are still in a trial-and-error phase of figuring out which use cases actually work.
  • The agents that create real value are the ones with business context: your data, your history, your constraints. Without it, an agent can only give generic advice, not decisions your company can act on.

Amber Roberts, Staff Technical Marketing Manager at Databricks, has spent the last several years watching how AI actually gets used inside organizations, not just how it's pitched. In this conversation, she talks through why "faster" is the wrong way to think about agentic AI, why so many companies are struggling to show ROI on their AI investments, and what has to be true for an AI agent to be useful at work instead of just impressive in a demo.

Most conversations about AI productivity are still about speed: doing the same tasks faster. Why is that the wrong lens for thinking about agentic AI, and what other KPIs should teams consider?

Amber Roberts: Productivity is tied to whatever a team's actual KPIs are, and that's different depending on where you sit. For some teams, the work is detail-oriented and speed isn't the biggest issue. For others, latency is the whole ballgame. Even the word "speed" means different things: speed of development versus speed of inference, for example.

Engineering productivity and marketing productivity aren't the same thing, and they shouldn't be measured the same way. So I'd push back on the idea that there's one right KPI to swap in. It depends on the team, and honestly, it depends on the person. Someone who's learning a domain from scratch is going to use AI differently, and value different things, than someone who already knows exactly what they want to build and just wants to automate the tedious parts.

I'm skeptical of headlines that go all in on "this is the wrong way to think about it." There's a lot of gray areas. Even people on the same team can have different priorities for what they want out of AI, depending on their own expertise.

There's a growing body of research showing companies are adopting AI fast but struggling to show real ROI. Why does that gap exist, and what does it reveal about how most organizations are deploying AI agents today?

Amber Roberts: The people buying AI and the people using it day to day are often different people. The buyers don't want to be late to the game. Their job depends on staying at the cutting edge of technology, even if they're not the ones implementing it. If they see competitors buying and deploying AI, they're going to want to make a deal happen. That's true of any new technology: nobody wants to be the one left behind.

Then, over six months to a few years, you start to see whether it actually built ROI, whether it was worth what was spent. That's the phase a lot of organizations are in right now: looking at what they bought, rolling it out broadly, and figuring out which use cases it's effective for. A lot of it is trial and error. But that trial and error is still better than being six months behind the competition.

How do you define productivity in an agentic world, and how is that different from how enterprises have measured it for the last 20 years?

Amber Roberts: The classic definition of productivity is how effectively inputs like labor, time, and capital turn into outputs like goods and services. What's interesting is that AI doesn't output a good, it outputs a service, optimizing something behind the scenes.

The key shift is this: productivity used to be measured by how much work one person could do. Now it's how much work a person can do with a team of assistants at their disposal. We see this even in how we evaluate people, in interviews or take-home assessments. It's no longer impressive to see how much someone produced alone in four hours, because there's a visible difference between that and what someone produces when they're leveraging AI well. That's the new baseline. But it doesn't replace deep knowledge of the subject matter. It just means the same instinct, the same taste, the same expertise, is now applied at a different scale.

Where I see the biggest jump is when people take everything that used to eat their day, the recurring, schedulable, "hire an assistant to do this" work, and automate it so they can focus on the harder, more creative parts of the job. The parts that require actual pushback and judgment, because AI's default mode is agreeable. It'll say "sounds good" to almost anything. That's useful for an assistant, but it's also exactly why the parts of a job that require someone to argue, to push back, to say "no, that's not right," matter more now, not less.

That's also the part that gets missed when people report productivity gains without a quality metric attached. Productivity is technically linked to efficiency, and it assumes you're not sacrificing quality to get there. If a company says they're 40% more efficient, that's really only meaningful if quality held steady. Otherwise you might just be taking the same amount of time to produce the same result, with more moving parts. That tracks with what we're seeing in content specifically: when you push volume up, without extra attention to the details that make something good, quality tends to slip. The tools don't always keep up.

A lot of AI tools can execute a task. What does it actually mean for an agent to "understand business context," and why does that matter more than speed?

Amber Roberts: I think about it like comparing an AI agent to a real human assistant. If you ask an assistant to do something and they don't have your context, your schedule, or a sense of what's happened over the last few months, they can't do the job well. Imagine asking someone to plan an event with no guest list, no inventory, no record of what was done last time, what worked, what didn't, who the vendors are and what they specialize in. You can't just swap that out. That's exactly why people with deep institutional knowledge are so hard to replace: it's far more expensive to lose that person and train someone new than it is to keep them.

That's where the value of business context comes in. You can get a lot of nice demos of "here's how you build this thing," with genuinely good generic instructions. But if you ask, "how do I build an addition onto my house," a generic AI tool will explain how additions generally work. It won't know your zip code, your local building codes, your city's ordinances. It has no information specific to your situation. And that's basically useless if what you're actually trying to build is something for your company, which is the entire reason you'd want AI at work in the first place.

REPORT

The agentic AI playbook for the enterprise

What are some examples of high-value, repeatable use cases emerging right now?

Amber Roberts: Honestly, there are too many to point to one. Engineering is a good example: scheduling jobs, or using something like Genie Spaces so you don't have to be an engineer to understand the code, you can just type in a question and get slides, documentation, and context back, including who else in the organization is already working on the same problem.

But it's really across every function: health, marketing, sales, finance. Every industry, and every team within it, has automated workflows that used to take a long time and don't anymore. It's a genuinely novel moment. There are opportunities that just haven't been touched or thought of yet, which makes this a pretty unique space to be working in right now.

A concrete example: I recently had to step in for a colleague managing speaker confirmations ahead of a conference. The manual version of that process is emailing each speaker individually, or at best sending out a form and manually compiling responses. Instead, I set up an agent to message all the speakers, log their responses, and flag who hadn't confirmed. A second agent reviewed the outstanding responses and followed up automatically. By the time I checked in, all 137 speakers had been contacted and confirmed, aside from two who happened to be on parental leave. That's the kind of repeatable, cross-functional task that's ripe for this right now.

How should enterprise leaders measure whether an agentic deployment is working? What metrics or signals should replace old productivity measures like tickets closed or hours saved?

Amber Roberts: I don't think traditional metrics go away, they're still how most organizations define success. Engineers especially aren't going to be convinced something's working unless they see their existing metrics improve. So you have to start there: if a task used to take an hour and an agent can do it in five minutes, that's the kind of result that actually convinces people.

Hours saved, tickets closed, these still matter, and they keep a human in the loop. What changes is what you add on top. You can bring in AI-specific metrics: a third-party LLM acting as a judge against criteria you define. For something like a chatbot, you'd still track resolution time and user satisfaction, but now you can also check for correctness, hallucinations, tone, and flag edge cases or anomalies automatically, instead of manually sifting through every piece of feedback yourself.

What's the most common mistake you see organizations make when they try to scale agentic AI, the thing that turns "faster" into "faster in the wrong direction"?

Amber Roberts: The biggest mistake is trying to scale something before it's working well. A few examples go well, people get excited, and the instinct is "let's scale this." But "scale" has become a bit of a buzzword. The real question is: what specifically do you want to see happen? It has to be evaluated use case by use case. Sometimes the thing doesn't need to be scaled out at all.

A lot of the time, what looks like a scaling problem is actually a readiness problem: it took a lot of iteration just to get one instance working well, and that gets overlooked. It's the same pattern as when a team says, "we have all this data, let's build on it," without checking whether it's the right data. Other times, it's an infrastructure gap. Demos from smaller startups can look great and make scaling look simple, but without the infrastructure to support it, there's nothing to scale against. That's a lot of what optimization work behind the scenes is about: building the infrastructure that makes scaling possible in the first place, not just promising that it will happen.

What does "a day's work" look like for a knowledge worker five years from now, and what has to be true organizationally for that to happen well?

Amber Roberts: I genuinely can't predict that with confidence. I couldn't have told you two years ago where we'd be today. I read something I wrote two years ago recently and barely recognized how far off it already was.

What I do think holds true is that critical thinking is more important now than it's ever been. There used to be a baseline of trust when you received a document, a video, or a piece of work: you could be nitpicky about specific details, but you generally trusted the source. Now you genuinely don't know what you're getting. You have to go into everything, before you even review it, assuming it could be AI-generated, and AI-generated without context, meaning it could be using outdated information, wrong information, or even a competitor's information without anyone realizing it.

That means everyone is going to have to stay ready to critically evaluate everything they see and everything they put out. I don't think "too polished" reads as trustworthy anymore. People are going to start treating anything that sounds too agreeable, too smooth, as a signal that it might be AI-generated without real judgment behind it. Which is exactly why having actual experts and advocates in the loop, people who know enough to push back, is going to matter more, not less, as this gets more capable.

The real measure of productivity Across every question, the same idea kept surfacing: agentic AI doesn't make old measures of productivity obsolete, it makes them incomplete. Hours saved and tickets closed still matter, but they only tell you what got faster, not what got better. The organizations getting real value aren't the ones chasing speed for its own sake. They're the ones giving agents the business context to make good decisions, keeping humans in the loop for judgment and pushback, and being honest about when something is ready to scale versus when it just looks good in a demo.

entries.content:
Debuts with the highest initial placement of any new vendor in the Magic Quadrant’’s 20+ year history.

by Chao Cai, Kayli Berlin and Miranda Luna

  • Databricks achieved the highest debut performance ever in the more than 20 year history of the Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Analytics and BI Platforms.
  • Databricks was recognized as a Visionary, achieving one of the highest scores for "Completeness of Vision" among all evaluated vendors.
  • Explore how Databricks AI/BI, Genie, and the Data + AI Platform are driving the market shift toward converged platforms, agentic analytics, and centralized semantics.

We are incredibly excited to announce that Databricks has made its inaugural appearance in the Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Analytics and Business Intelligence (ABI) Platforms 2026. Databricks debuted in the quadrant as a "Visionary". We also achieved one of the highest "Completeness of Vision" scores among all vendors evaluated.

This marks the highest debut performance any vendor has ever had in the 20+ year history of this Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ report. We believe this recognition validates our core thesis: the fundamental nature of BI has changed, and the future belongs to data platforms that inherently fuse analytics with enterprise AI. Legacy BI tools were built for a different era: one defined by rigid data models and heavy data extracts that tied data teams up with answering basic questions, rather than freeing them to drive high-value, strategic analysis. The days of locking data into proprietary BI silos to build backward-looking dashboards have already ended.

Gartner’s Hype Cycle for Analytics and Business Intelligence highlights this massive change in the industry. We see our strong placement in the Magic Quadrant as a direct result of our ability to deliver on three major trends reshaping businesses today:

  • Data & AI Platform Convergence: Bringing different tools together into a single platform reduces everyday complexity, streamlines workflows, and makes it easier to scale AI infrastructure. This union enables the global boom in AI adoption by ensuring company-wide data use is consistent and governed.
  • Agentic Analytics: AI agents are transforming data management, analysis, and decision-making. By automating manual workflows, they help organizations move faster and drive greater business value.
  • Semantics at the Core: A unified, governed semantic layer gives every human and agent the same definitions, context, and rules. It is critical to safely scale autonomous agents and agent-to-agent workflows. Without it, conflicting interpretations create too much risk of error.

For decades, traditional BI forced a bad tradeoff: copy data into separate systems—fracturing governance and analyzing stale information—or pay extra for bespoke engines to query it in place. Augmented BI did not change that foundation; it simply layered forecasts and anomaly detection onto the same incomplete data picture.

Truly agentic BI requires eliminating every information silo so agents can reason over the full, governed context. Agents are only as smart as the part of the picture they can access, and incomplete context creates unreliable answers. That is why Databricks integrates BI directly into the lakehouse. With Genie and AI/BI, agents work from the same complete, governed source of truth—without extracts, duplicated data, or a separate BI layer.

Databricks’ agentic analytics offering eliminates manual bottlenecks by automating complex workflows, empowering teams to move faster from insight to autonomous action and drive significantly greater business value. Databricks AI/BI pushes business intelligence beyond basic queries into dynamic, action-oriented workflows. Genie One, our data-smart AI coworker, seamlessly connects insights to smart actions, eliminating the manual steps typically required between finding a data point and acting on it. Furthermore, Genie Agents allow teams to turn simple prompts into shareable, independent agents capable of reasoning through both structured data tables and messy, unstructured documents. By taking autonomous action to manage schedules, generate documents, and execute complex multi-step workflows across your business tools, these capabilities drastically reduce manual toil.

Trusted AI and BI start with a shared understanding of your business. Unity Catalog Business Semantics lets you define metrics, dimensions, relationships, and business terms once, then govern and apply them consistently across dashboards, analytics, and agents. Genie Ontology builds on that foundation by automatically organizing context from data, queries, dashboards, pipelines, and connected tools into a living map of how your business works. Together, they help Genie know where to look, what to trust, and how to answer complex questions with complete, governed business context.

BI has already changed. It is no longer just about building dashboards and reports in advance for a specific part of the business. The new model is dynamic and proactive. Insights are pushed to you, not just pulled when you ask for them. Anyone can dig deeper from a high-level trend down to the real truth behind it, and AI agents make sure every answer tells the full story.

That new world is exactly where we are ahead with Genie and Databricks AI/BI. Business users rely on it every day to see key trends, understand what changed and why, and decide what to do about it instantly. By bringing insights directly to where you work—whether that is through mobile apps, Slack, Microsoft Teams, or custom AI assistants—we are truly putting data in the hands of everyone in the company.

We are grateful to the thousands of customers who have partnered with us to push the limits of what is possible with their data. Being named a Visionary with the highest debut performance in the history of the Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Analytics and BI Platforms is an incredible milestone, and it is only the beginning.

Ready to see the future of AI-driven analytics in action? Learn more about AI/BI here.

entries.title: What is HTAP? A plain-English guide to hybrid transactional/analytical processing
entries.summary: Consider a payment system processing a purchase. Before approving the transaction,...
entries.content:
Consider a payment system processing a purchase. Before approving the transaction, a fraud model may need to evaluate it against the account's recent activity. But if that transactional data must first move from the transactional database to a data warehouse for analysis, even a short delay can make the result less useful.

Hybrid Transactional/Analytical Processing (HTAP) brings transaction processing and analytics closer together to address this problem. An HTAP database lets you run analytical queries on operational data while it is still current, without waiting for a batch data pipeline to move it into a separate analytical system.

In this guide, you'll learn how HTAP works, the architectural tradeoffs involved, and where it fits in a modern data architecture. You'll also see how different HTAP systems approach transactional and analytical workloads, how HTAP compares with Lake Transactional/Analytical Processing (LTAP), and what to consider when evaluating and adopting either approach.

  • HTAP brings transactional and analytical processing closer together so applications can run analytics on fresh transactional data.
  • Different HTAP architectures involve different trade-offs in performance, isolation, data consistency, and freshness.
  • Choose the architecture based on your workload. LTAP provides greater separation between transactional and analytical compute while both operate on the same data.

HTAP stands for Hybrid Transactional/Analytical Processing. Gartner coined the term in 2014 to describe architectures that bring online transaction processing (OLTP) and online analytical processing (OLAP) together within an integrated database system. Gartner's original framing of hybrid transaction/analytical processing argued that combining the two would create opportunities for dramatic business innovation, because decisions could be OLTP handles high volumes of small, frequent transactional operations that keep applications running, such as creating an order, processing a payment, or updating an account. OLAP processes complex queries over large datasets to calculate metrics, identify patterns, and answer analytical questions.made on the latest transactions rather than on yesterday's extract.

HTAP brings these workloads closer together, giving analytical queries access to current operational data without depending entirely on a separate batch ETL pipeline. For many operational analytics use cases, HTAP systems can reduce or remove the need for ETL processes, cut down the number of data copies teams maintain, and move closer to a single source of truth for both operational and analytical systems. In the most integrated designs, OLTP and OLAP capabilities live in a single system rather than in two products stitched together.

Bringing OLTP and OLAP workloads closer together does not mean they have to run in exactly the same way. HTAP architectures therefore differ in how they combine OLTP and OLAP capabilities while preserving the characteristics each workload needs. Two common approaches are:

  • Converged HTAP: Runs transactional and analytical workloads through a single database engine. The workloads may use different indexes, storage formats, or execution paths, but they share much of the same database.
  • Composed HTAP: Uses separate transactional and analytical engines within an integrated architecture. The engines may share a storage layer or propagate changes through replication while remaining optimized for their respective workloads.

A converged engine avoids the need to synchronize independent query engines, but it must prevent analytical operations from interfering with latency-sensitive transactions. A composed architecture provides greater freedom to optimize and isolate each workload, but it must coordinate data versions and keep the analytical path sufficiently fresh.

In both cases, the central HTAP challenge is the same: provide analytical access to operational data quickly enough to be useful without compromising the performance and reliability of transactional workloads.

OLTP and OLAP have different access patterns. Transactional queries typically read or update a small number of complete rows. OLTP databases therefore rely on row-based storage, selective indexes, efficient concurrency control, and predictable latency, often measured in milliseconds. Most transactional databases are relational databases tuned to keep that latency low even under heavy concurrency.

Analytical queries, by contrast, often scan millions of rows across a subset of columns to calculate metrics or identify patterns. OLAP databases use columnar storage because a column store improves compression and reduces the amount of unnecessary data read during large scans and aggregations. OLAP systems can tolerate longer latency for complex queries, trading seconds of response time for the ability to analyze far more data.

Optimizing OLTP and OLAP systems separately therefore made practical sense, but it introduced a new problem: the delay caused by data movement between them. Operational data typically had to be copied out of the OLTP system and into a data warehouse or other analytical database before it could be analyzed. Transactions and analytics processing ran on different schedules, on different hardware, against different copies of the data. Traditional architectures that separate OLTP and OLAP systems in this way build latency into every analytical answer.

As requirements for fresher data grew, data teams started assembling their own custom systems to close the gap. Change data capture feeds, stream processors, cloud data warehouses, cloud data lakes, and real-time query layers became the building blocks of today's disaggregated data stack. Each component solved a specific problem, but every additional hop added cost, operational effort, and another place where data consistency could break.

HTAP addresses that delay while preserving the performance benefits of workload-specific optimization.

An HTAP architecture provides paths for both transactional and analytical workloads while keeping operational data available for analysis with minimal delay. The exact design varies by system, but the architecture generally includes transaction processing, analytical processing, workload-specific data representations, and a mechanism for keeping those representations synchronized, as shown below.

The transactional path handles frequent application reads and writes, such as creating orders, updating accounts, or recording payments. These transactional workloads typically operate on small numbers of rows and require low latency, efficient concurrency control, and reliable transaction guarantees.

HTAP systems commonly use row-oriented storage engines, indexes, caches, and a write-ahead log designed to serve these operational access patterns efficiently and durably.

The analytical path handles analytical queries that scan, filter, join, and aggregate larger amounts of data. Columnar representations are commonly used because analytical queries often need a subset of columns across many rows, and they are what make fast OLAP queries possible on operational data.

Depending on the HTAP design, analytical processing may run in the same database engine as transactions or on separate analytical compute. Separating the compute paths allows each workload to use execution resources optimized for its access patterns, so the system can add analytical capabilities without slowing OLTP systems down. Many HTAP systems also use intelligent query optimization, where the optimizer decides whether a query should read from the row store, the column store, or both.

HTAP systems may maintain more than one representation of the same data. A row-oriented storage engine can serve transactional access while a columnar storage engine supports analytical scans and aggregations.

These representations may exist within one database system or across separate transactional and analytical components. Some architectures also decouple compute from storage and use object storage alongside caches, logs, or other services.

When transactional and analytical processing use different storage engines or components, committed changes need a path from the transactional side to the analytical side. Systems can use mechanisms such as change data capture (CDC), replication of the write-ahead log, shared logs, or shared storage to propagate those changes.

The result is an analytical view that can incorporate recently committed transactions without requiring the traditional process of periodically extracting an entire dataset into a separate analytical system. How quickly those changes become visible depends on the architecture and its consistency guarantees.

Bringing transactional and analytical workloads closer together introduces tradeoffs in how data is stored and processed. Where those costs appear depends on the architecture, but HTAP databases struggle with the same core problem: optimizing for both OLTP and OLAP workloads at once. Four challenges are common.

Maintaining analytical data alongside frequent transactional writes creates additional work. Because many HTAP systems store data in two formats, updates may generate deltas or require refresh and compaction, increasing compute, I/O, and storage usage even when that work stays off the transaction path.

When OLTP workloads and OLAP workloads share resources, large analytical queries can push transaction latency from milliseconds to seconds. Separate compute provides stronger isolation, but you still need to account for shared bottlenecks such as storage, networking, and coordination services.

Transactional and analytical paths may not advance at the same rate. You need to decide how quickly committed changes must become available for analysis and what data consistency guarantees the workload requires. Greater freshness typically requires tighter coordination between the two paths, and every HTAP architecture manages some tension between synchronization and isolation rather than eliminating it.

Supporting mixed workloads can mean managing multiple data representations, execution paths, resource policies, and synchronization mechanisms. Query optimizers must also choose good execution plans across two storage formats. You need to account for that complexity when monitoring, scaling, troubleshooting, and recovering the system.

When evaluating an HTAP solution, test transactional and analytical workloads together under conditions that reflect your production environment. Measure whether transaction latency, analytical performance, and data freshness remain within your requirements as both workloads run concurrently.

Criterion What to test
OLTP p99 latency under mixed load Check whether p99 (99th-percentile) transaction latency stays within your target as analytical load increases.
Analytical performance at scale Test scan and aggregation performance as your data volume, query complexity, and concurrency grow.
Freshness and consistency Measure how quickly committed changes become queryable and whether the consistency guarantees meet your requirements, including when the analytical path falls behind.
Cost under mixed load Measure compute, storage, caching, replication, network, and data-transfer costs at traffic levels representative of your workload.
Failure and recovery Test how queries behave during failures, whether correctness is maintained under degraded conditions, how backlogs grow, and how quickly the system recovers.
Operational overhead Consider how much effort you will need for tuning, monitoring, capacity planning, workload management, and incident response.

Use production-like data, query patterns, volumes, and concurrency wherever possible. Include bursty writes, skewed data, traffic spikes, and demanding analytical queries so you can see how the system behaves under the conditions it will actually face.

You can see the different ways HTAP systems separate transactional and analytical workloads in systems such as TiDB, AlloyDB, and Databricks Lakebase. Each takes a different approach to transaction processing, analytical processing, and the data path between them.

TiDB illustrates a composed HTAP architecture. In 2020, PingCAP published a VLDB paper describing TiDB as a Raft-based HTAP database, and its decoupled architecture integrates row and column storage for hybrid workloads. Transactional workloads use TiKV, a row-based storage engine, while TiFlash maintains a columnar representation for analytical queries. TiDB's optimizer can route queries to TiKV, TiFlash, or both, with the two paths running on separate nodes for greater workload isolation.

TiFlash receives replicas asynchronously through the Raft log but checks whether it has reached the data version required by a query to provide snapshot isolation. When evaluating this approach, consider how replication lag affects analytical latency and throughput during sustained transactional writes.

AlloyDB takes a more converged approach. It operates with a transparent in-memory columnar engine that accelerates analytical operations such as scans, joins, and aggregations. The engine can run on the primary instance or on read-pool instances for greater workload isolation. Google states that AlloyDB delivers up to 100x faster analytical queries than standard PostgreSQL.

When evaluating this approach, consider how much of your workload can use the columnar path. Unsupported operations or data unavailable in the columnar engine may fall back to the row-oriented path, while frequent updates can require columnar data to be refreshed. Test columnar coverage and performance using representative query and update patterns.

Lakebase with LTAP takes the separation between transactional and analytical workloads further. Rather than serving both through the same database engine, it keeps their compute independent while connecting them through a shared data layer. Postgres compute can remain optimized for low-latency transactions, while analytical compute processes the same operational data without placing analytical workloads on the primary database.

This separation also allows the two sides to scale independently. Transactional capacity can follow application traffic, while analytical capacity can follow query demand, without requiring one workload to provision resources for the other. For live reads, analytical compute reads the bulk of data from the columnar copy in object storage, fetches only the current log position from Postgres, and merges any very recent changes from the pageserver to provide a transactionally consistent view, without placing analytical workload on the primary Postgres instance.

HTAP has been pitched as the next big DB architecture more than once. In practice, it is a good fit when the value of your analysis depends on access to fresh operational data. Start by asking how much delay your workload can tolerate. If data becomes less useful while moving from a transactional system to a separate analytical system, reducing that delay may justify an HTAP architecture.

That question matters more as emerging workloads such as AI agents and real-time personalization need current state and historical context at the same time. It is also why the conversation has shifted away from tightly coupled warehouses toward modular lakes built on open formats, where transactional and analytical systems can share data without forcing every workload into one engine.

Real-time business intelligence You need dashboards and metrics to reflect recent operational activity. Freshness, analytical concurrency, and transaction latency
Operational analytics You use analytical results to inform an active workflow or decision. Consistency, query latency, and workload isolation

Choose the architecture based on how much freshness and workload isolation you need. Converged HTAP can work well when transactional and analytical workloads can safely share an operating environment. Composed HTAP provides stronger compute isolation when synchronization can still keep analytical data current enough for your workload.

Keep OLTP and OLAP separate when your analytical workloads can tolerate some delay. Historical analysis, model training, advanced analytics, and regulatory reporting can often remain on a dedicated OLAP database or in cloud data warehouses, especially when you need to protect transactional latency and availability through stronger workload isolation.

Consider your existing architecture as well. If your CDC or ETL data processing already meets your freshness, performance, reliability, and cost requirements, moving to HTAP may introduce migration risk and operational complexity without enough benefit. HTAP is most valuable when reducing data delay solves a specific application or business problem.

Once you have validated that an HTAP architecture can meet your workload requirements, adopt it incrementally. Set clear success criteria at each stage and make sure you can return to the existing path if those criteria are not met.

A practical migration sequence is:

  • Map your workloads and dependencies: Identify the applications, queries, pipelines, and downstream consumers involved. Separate transactional and analytical workloads from those that genuinely need both.
  • Set your guardrails: Define acceptable thresholds for transaction latency, analytical performance, freshness, correctness, availability, and cost. Decide in advance what would cause you to pause or roll back.
  • Start with analytical reads: Where possible, run the existing and new analytical paths in parallel. Compare results, freshness, and performance before the new path affects application behavior.
  • Shift traffic gradually: Move suitable workloads in stages while monitoring the new path and its effect on transactional performance.
  • Test failure and recovery: Verify what happens when synchronization falls behind, components fail, or traffic returns to the previous path. Test these procedures before you depend on them in production.
  • Migrate writes only if needed: If adoption changes your system of record, first validate durability, schema evolution, downstream dependencies, and rollback behavior.

Use the migration to review your schemas, indexes, and access patterns. HTAP can change how you store and query data, but it cannot compensate for a data model that does not fit your workload.

HTAP can reduce the gap between transactions and analytics, but the right architecture depends on your workload. Start with the transaction latency, analytical performance, freshness, consistency, and isolation your application requires, then test those requirements together under representative mixed load.

HTAP stands for Hybrid Transactional/Analytical Processing. It is a database architecture that brings online transaction processing (OLTP) and online analytical processing (OLAP) together, allowing applications to analyze operational data while it is still current.

An HTAP database supports both transactional and analytical workloads. Converged systems handle both through a single database engine, while composed systems use separate transactional and analytical engines connected through shared storage, replication, or other synchronization mechanisms.

In databases, HTAP reduces the traditional separation between operational and analytical systems. It gives analytical queries access to fresher transactional data without relying entirely on moving that data through a separate batch ETL pipeline first.

OLTP databases process high volumes of small transactions using row-oriented storage and low-latency access. OLAP databases run complex queries over large datasets using columnar storage, accepting longer latency in exchange for efficient scans and aggregations.

LTAP stands for Lake Transactional/Analytical Processing. It serves both transactional and analytical workloads from a unified storage layer in the lake, under one governance model, removing the CDC and replication pipelines teams traditionally maintain to keep separate systems in sync. This allows each workload to optimize and scale independently while operating on a common data foundation.
